title: Data-Efficient and Interpretable Tabular Anomaly Detection

problem.claim: Anomaly detection must support real-world applications where small quantities of labeled data may be available and stakeholders need to understand why samples are identified as anomalies.

gap.claim: Most existing anomaly detection methods cannot incorporate small amounts of labeled data and are not interpretable.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes DIAD, an anomaly detection framework that adapts Generalized Additive Models with a partial identification objective to handle noisy or heterogeneous features.
DIAD incorporates a small amount of labeled data for semi-supervised anomaly detection.
DIAD provides explainability capabilities for its anomaly predictions.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe DIAD as a novel anomaly detection framework.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that DIAD outperforms previous work in unsupervised and semi-supervised settings across multiple datasets.
The authors report explainability capabilities concerning the rationale for predicting samples as anomalies.

narrative_sequence.summary: Anomaly detection is important across numerous applications.
The paper focuses on labeled-data integration and interpretability as critical but understudied requirements for real-world anomaly detection.
DIAD adapts Generalized Additive Models with a partial identification objective and can use small amounts of labeled data.
The authors report superiority over prior work on multiple datasets in unsupervised and semi-supervised settings.
The paper presents DIAD's explainability capabilities and rationale for anomaly predictions.

source_observation.claim: Small quantities of labeled data may be available in practice and can improve anomaly detection accuracy.

interpretation.claim: Anomaly detection systems should support semi-supervised learning when limited labels are available.

application.claim: When deploying anomaly detection, evaluate whether a method can use sparse labels without requiring a fully labeled dataset.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify how much labeled data is required or how performance changes with label quantity.

source_observation.claim: The paper links interpretability to stakeholders' ability to understand why samples are predicted as anomalies.

interpretation.claim: Interpretability can be treated as a deployment requirement for anomaly detection rather than only a secondary analysis feature.

application.claim: For stakeholder-facing anomaly detection, inspect whether predictions include an understandable rationale.

exception.claim: The abstract does not describe the form or fidelity of the explanations.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the datasets or report quantitative performance results.
The abstract does not specify the partial identification objective or model implementation details.
The abstract does not quantify the amount or quality of labeled data used.
The abstract does not provide independent verification of the reported superiority.
